entities.summary:
The Battle of Lechfeld was a pivotal event in European history, fought on August 10, 955, between the German Empire and the Hungarian tribes. Led by King Otto I, the German forces decisively defeated the Hungarians, marking a turning point in the gradual decline of the Magyar power and setting the stage for the rise of medieval Germany.

The battle took place in the Lechfeld, a region in present-day Bavaria, Germany, where the German forces had been gathering to counter the Hungarian invasion. The German army, led by Otto I and his brother Henry II, employed a clever tactic of deploying their fighting men in a triangular formation, with the flanks protected by cavalry and the center held by infantry. This innovative formation allowed the Germans to withstand the initial Hungarian charge and then launch a successful counterattack, routing the Hungarian forces and securing a crushing victory.

The Battle of Lechfeld had significant consequences for the balance of power in Europe. It marked the beginning of the end of Hungarian dominance in Central Europe and paved the way for the rise of the Holy Roman Empire, which would go on to play a major role in shaping European politics for centuries to come. The battle also had a lasting impact on the development of medieval warfare, as it showcased the effectiveness of the triangular formation and the use of cavalry as a key component of battle tactics.

As the German historian Voltaire once noted, 'The Battle of Lechfeld was a turning point in the history of the world, marking the beginning of the decline of the Magyars and the rise of the German Empire.'
